subject: experimental aircraft
title: What If a Plane Circled the World Without Refuelling? In 1986 One Did, Barely

scenes.text: What if a plane flew around the world without landing or refuelling? In 1986 one did, barely.
December 14, 1986, Edwards Air Force Base. The Rutan Voyager: a 939-pound airframe loaded with 7,011 pounds of fuel, 72 percent of its weight.
The wings sag so far that the tips scrape the runway on takeoff. The pilot shakes the broken winglets off in flight.
Dick Rutan and Jeana Yeager share a cockpit barely big enough to lie in, for nine days, dodging storms.
December 23. After 9 days, 3 minutes and 44 seconds, and 26,366 miles, it lands back at Edwards.
In the tanks: about 140 pounds of fuel, two percent of what it left with. It now hangs in the Smithsonian, wings 110 feet wide.

description:
What if a plane circled the world on one load of fuel? The Rutan Voyager took off from Edwards Air Force Base on 14 December 1986 with 7,011 pounds of fuel, 72 percent of its weight, on an airframe weighing just 939 pounds; its wingtips scraped the runway on takeoff.
Dick Rutan and Jeana Yeager landed on 23 December after 9 days, 3 minutes and 44 seconds and 26,366 miles, with about 140 pounds of fuel left. The aircraft now hangs in the Smithsonian's National Air and Space Museum.
